why-vector.title: Why flight computers need dynamic arrays
body: In previous missions, we stored telemetry in fixed arrays such as `int temps[5]` and `int map[3][3]`. Static arrays are fast and predictable, but they require knowing the exact element count at compile time.

Now Scout drone **IZLŪKS 'Sigma'** enters uncharted volcanic lava tubes beneath Mawrth Vallis. As Sigma navigates subterranean chasms, its lidar logs navigational beacon coordinates dynamically. Before entering the chasm, the flight computer cannot know whether the route will require 4 waypoints, 85 waypoints, or 300 waypoints.

If you declare a static array `int path[50];`, finding 51 waypoints will crash your program or corrupt critical memory. Conversely, reserving `int path[10000];` wastes valuable RAM if only 5 waypoints are detected.
C++ solves this with the dynamic array container: `std::vector` (provided by `#include <vector>`):
- **Dynamic capacity.** A vector starts empty and automatically expands in computer memory as new elements are added.
- **Contiguous storage.** Just like a traditional array, vector elements are stored in consecutive memory cells, granting instant $O(1)$ indexed access.
- **Self-tracking size.** A vector knows its own element count at all times via `.size()`.

archive.title: Dynamic containers vs static buffers in space exploration software
archive.body: In early spacecraft avionics, dynamic memory allocation was banned because heap fragmentation could cause missions to fail during critical maneuvers. However, modern planetary robotic systems—such as NASA's Mars 2020 Perseverance rover and ESA's ExoMars rover—rely on hybrid memory architectures. For high-level autonomous science planners and terrain-relative navigation (TRN) image matchers, C++ `std::vector` is widely used with pre-allocated capacity (`vec.reserve(expected_capacity)`). This combines the flexibility of dynamic containers with the latency guarantees of static memory buffers.
sources: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, 'C++ Coding Standard for Flight Software'
IEEE Aerospace Conference, 'Autonomous Navigation and Science Target Selection for Mars Rovers'

vector-syntax-and-push.title: Declaring vectors and appending with push_back
compareCaptions: Correct dynamic growth: push_back dynamically appends elements to vector
Undefined memory access: writing to index 0 of an empty vector crashes
body: To use vectors, include the `<vector>` library header. The declaration specifies the element type inside angle brackets `<type>`:
To append an element to the end of the vector, call the `.push_back(value)` member function:

```cpp
waypoints.push_back(120); // Adds 120 at index 0 (size becomes 1)
waypoints.push_back(180); // Adds 180 at index 1 (size becomes 2)
```
You can inspect the current count of elements using `.size()`, and access elements with familiar array brackets `[i]`:

```cpp
cout << waypoints.size(); // Prints: 2
cout << waypoints[0];      // Prints: 120
```

!> **The empty vector indexing trap.** When a vector is declared without an initial size (`vector<int> v;`), it contains **0 elements**. Writing `v[0] = 50;` is illegal out-of-bounds access! Always populate empty vectors using `.push_back()`, which allocates memory for the new element before writing to it.

predict-vector-push.title: Trace vector growth and pop_back
body: Trace the execution of this navigational waypoint logger.
Determine the final output printed to the terminal console.
predict-vector-push.explain: Initially, `waypoints` receives 100, 250, and 400 (size 3). Then `pop_back()` removes the last element (400), reducing the size to 2. Next, `push_back(350)` adds 350 to the end. The vector now holds `[100, 250, 350]` with `size() == 3`. Index 1 holds `250`. Output is `3 250`.

vector-input-loop.title: Lidar elevation stream logger
vector-input-loop.task:
Program Scout drone Sigma's dynamic elevation logger:
1. Read sample count `int n` from `cin`.
2. Declare an empty integer vector `vector<int> elevations;`.
3. In a `for` loop running `n` times: read `int val` from `cin` and append it to `elevations` using `elevations.push_back(val);`.
4. In a second `for` loop from `i = 0` to `i < elevations.size()`: print `ELEVATION #` followed by `i`, `: `, `elevations[i]`, and a newline.
vector-input-loop.hint: Declare `vector<int> elevations;` before the input loop. In the second loop, use `elevations.size()` to iterate safely through all elements.
vector-input-loop.solutionNote: Using push_back allows the vector to accommodate any input size n dynamically.

find-vector-size-bug.title: Identify out-of-bounds vector loop
body: This program initializes a 3-element coordinate vector and attempts to print each coordinate.
However, the loop condition causes a boundary crash on the final pass. Click on the line containing the bug.
find-vector-size-bug.explain: Line 7 uses `i <= coords.size()`. In a vector with 3 elements, `coords.size()` is 3, so valid indices are strictly 0, 1, and 2. When `i` reaches 3, `coords[3]` accesses out-of-bounds memory! The condition should use strict inequality `i < coords.size()`.

vector-sum-and-peak.title: Seismic signal peak and sum analyzer
vector-sum-and-peak.task:
Program Sigma's acoustic echo processor:
1. Read total signal count `int count` from `cin`.
2. Read `count` integers into a `vector<int> signals;` using `.push_back()`.
3. In a `for` loop, compute the `sum` of all elements in `signals`.
4. In the same loop or a second pass, find the peak reading `max_signal` (initialized to `signals[0]`).
5. Print `TOTAL SIGNAL: ` followed by `sum` and a newline.
6. Print `PEAK SIGNAL: ` followed by `max_signal` and a newline.
vector-sum-and-peak.hint: Initialize `int sum = 0;` and `int max_signal = signals[0];`. Iterate from `i = 0` to `i < signals.size()` updating both.
vector-sum-and-peak.solutionNote: By initializing max_signal with signals[0], the peak detection works correctly even with negative readings.

predict-vector-empty.title: Vector empty status and stack operations
body: Trace this program utilizing `.empty()` and `.pop_back()` on a sensor stack.
Determine the exact string output printed to the console.
predict-vector-empty.explain: The stack pushes 5 and 15, then `pop_back()` removes 15. The vector now holds only `[5]`. The condition `!stack.empty()` is true because the vector contains 1 element. It outputs `ACTIVE `, `stack.size()` (1), ` VAL `, and `stack[0]` (5), printing `ACTIVE 1 VAL 5`.

drone-flight-path-logger.title: Sigma canyon trajectory audit
drone-flight-path-logger.task:
Program an autonomous canyon flight path auditor for Scout drone Sigma:
1. Read number of waypoints `int n` from `cin`.
2. In a loop, read `n` altitude values into `vector<int> altitudes;` using `.push_back()`.
3. Initialize counter `int high_altitude_count = 0;` and accumulator `int total_alt = 0;`.
4. In a `for` loop over `altitudes`: add each altitude to `total_alt`, and if `altitudes[i] >= 100`, increment `high_altitude_count`.
5. Print `WAYPOINTS LOGGED: ` followed by `altitudes.size()` and a newline.
6. Print `TOTAL ALTITUDE: ` followed by `total_alt` and a newline.
7. Print `HIGH ALTITUDE FIXES: ` followed by `high_altitude_count` and a newline.
drone-flight-path-logger.hint: Read all values with `altitudes.push_back(alt);` first, then run a traversal loop from `i = 0` to `i < altitudes.size()` to accumulate and count.
drone-flight-path-logger.solutionNote: This capstone combines dynamic collection, statistical aggregation, and condition filtering into a single aerospace workflow.

recap.title: Dynamic vectors recap
body: In this mission, you unlocked dynamic memory collections in C++ using `std::vector`:

| Feature | Static array (`int a[N]`) | Dynamic vector (`vector<int> v`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Header** | Built-in | `#include <vector>` |
| **Capacity** | Fixed at compile time | Grows dynamically at runtime |
| **Appending** | Cannot expand | `v.push_back(value)` |
| **Removing** | Cannot shrink | `v.pop_back()` |
| **Size query** | Must track separately | `v.size()` |
| **Emptiness** | No built-in test | `v.empty()` returns `true`/`false` |
| **Index access** | `a[i]` | `v[i]` or safe `v.at(i)` |
